activities.caption: true or false — how acquisition actually runs
activities.name: htlalEnginesJudge

statements.s: Nobody drilled you on the rules of your first language; you absorbed it from tens of thousands of hours of real use.
statements.why: You already know how languages are learned — the system assembled itself from meaningful contact.

statements.s: Comprehensible input means material just past your level — Krashen's i+1.
statements.why: Listening and reading slightly above what you already have, so the unknown sits inside known grammar.

statements.s: Talent decides more than how the hours are arranged.
statements.why: Talent is mostly hours, arranged well — input, spaced repetition, early speaking.

statements.s: Early speaking forces retrieval and exposes exactly the gaps worth learning next.
statements.why: Reaching for a word you have seen but never used fixes it more than ten more sightings.

activities.anchor: The gap between "can order dinner" and "can read a novel"
activities.caption: call the plateau's size
activities.name: htlalPlateauEstimate

config.prompt: Word families for knowing 98% of the words on a page — comfortable reading in a language like English?
config.why: Roughly 8,000–9,000 — the plateau between tourist talk and chapter books. The early words were frequent enough to meet thirty times a day; the late ones need deliberate hunting.
config.context: The top 1,000 words already cover the large majority of ordinary speech; the top 2,000–3,000 push past 90% of everyday text and talk.

activities.anchor: is the single highest-yield habit in the field
activities.caption: pick tonight's input
activities.name: htlalInputBranch

config.root: It is evening and you have thirty minutes of input. Three options are open.

start.text: Which one do you press play on?

choices.label: The prestige drama you follow at about a third
choices.feedback: Noise, not learning: too much unknown, nothing to hang context on.

choices.label: The episode you understand 80–90% of
choices.feedback: The story holds attention while the unknown 10–20% sits surrounded by known grammar.

choices.label: The children's cartoon you understand completely
choices.feedback: Comfort and no growth — nothing new to extract.

toohard.text: Step down to graded content — real stories rewritten with a limited vocabulary — until comprehension climbs.

choices.label: Pick again
choices.feedback: Slightly too hard, never hopelessly hard.

sweet.text: This is i+1: slightly past your level, every day.

choices.label: Make it a routine
choices.feedback: Daily, massive, slightly too hard — the best move there is.

tooeasy.text: Trade up a level — comfort teaches nothing new.

massive.text: Hours per week, not minutes: exposure volume is what drives the curve.

config.why: Slightly too hard, never hopelessly hard: the unknown word doing an inferable job inside known grammar is what gets absorbed.

activities.caption: find the line the grammar-table myth would love
activities.name: htlalGrammarSpot

config.prompt: One line of this summary misstates the research — click it:
lines: Grammar knowledge helps you notice patterns in input.
The patterns themselves are absorbed from contact, not memorised as rules.
Drill the grammar tables to automaticity — that is what acquisition is made of.
Perfect recitation of a verb form, then failure to use it mid-conversation.
The conversational system runs on absorbed chunks, not conscious grammar.
config.correction: Study grammar to understand what you hear; acquire grammar by hearing it.
config.why: Contact builds the conversational system; conscious rules only help you notice what contact delivers.

activities.anchor: memory decays exponentially, but each successful retrieval
activities.caption: which line is the SRS card?
activities.name: htlalCurveTrace

config.prompt: Two memories start today — which curve belongs to the card that gets pulled just as it begins to fade?
config.why: SRS schedules returns at 1 day, then 3, then 7, then 16 — each interval stretched by success, so 15–20 daily minutes maintain thousands of words.

activities.caption: pair each contrast case with the measured result
activities.name: htlalContrastMatch

config.prompt: Which new sounds will be easy? Pair each case with the measured outcome:

pairs.left: contrasts that map onto one you already make
pairs.right: two Zulu lateral fricatives differing in voicing — about 95% correct
Zulu clicks — about 80%, no old category in the way

pairs.left: two foreign sounds landing in a single native category
pairs.right: plosive versus implosive bilabial stops — about 65%, both resembling "b"

pairs.left: one lifelong category that must become two
pairs.right: Japanese speakers and English l versus r

config.why: Minimal-pair listening drills teach the ears the difference your native categories blur; shadowing then trains the mouth to produce it.

activities.anchor: learners who watch only outcomes quit
activities.caption: line up the survival rules
activities.name: htlalSystemOrder

config.prompt: The daily system that survives real life — order the rules:
items: Anchor each habit to an existing one — cards with the morning coffee, input on the commute
Track the inputs you control — hours listened, cards matured, sessions spoken
Once a week, name what was hard to say or understand
Turn each answer into next week's cards — failed conversations become the curriculum
config.why: The fragile part is the habit, not the willpower — and the scoreboard you control keeps you steady while progress lags weeks behind.

activities.caption: bet on what the streak bought
activities.name: htlalStreakPredict

config.q: A friend celebrates a 100-day streak in a gamified app. What has it actually guaranteed?
choices: Well-spaced review of the cards inside the app — nothing more
config.why: Apps are good at exactly one thing — spaced review of your cards. The bulk of hours must come from real shows, books and conversations, where the language lives.
